Learning Objectives
Identify the epidemiology and etiology of primary osteoarthritis of the wrist.
Identify the epidemiology and etiology of wrist arthritis secondary to scaphoid nonunion
advanced collapse/scapholunate advanced collapse.
Perform an appropriate physical examination and workup for patients in whom wrist arthritis
and/or scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse/scapholunate advanced collapse is suspected.
Describe the pathophysiology and resultant degenerative changes associated with scaphoid
nonunion advanced collapse/scapholunate advanced collapse.
Describe treatment options for wrist osteoarthritis and scaphoid nonunion advanced
collapse/scapholunate advanced collapse.

Anatomy
Knowledge of normal wrist anatomy facilitates understanding of primary (or idiopathic) and
secondary (posttraumatic, gout, calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate) osteoarthritis of the wrist
Osseous Anatomy
The carpus often is conceptualized as proximal and distal rows
Distal row
The trapezium, trapezoid, and capitate are fixed to the index and long finger metacarpals
and do not move.
The hamate is fixed to the capitate; however, the little and ring finger metacarpals have a
mobile articulation with the hamate that facilitates cupping of the hand.
Proximal row
The scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum form the mobile proximal row.
No muscles move these bones.
Their motions are a consequence of their shape and interconnections.

Osseous Anatomy
The wrist is a complex articulation, involving 15 bones including the pisiform (a sesamoid
in the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon that articulates with the hamate). The distal radius and
ulna articulate with the proximal row of the carpus, and the distal row articulates with
the five metacarpal bones. The proximal row of the carpus includes the scaphoid, lunate,
and triquetrum. The distal row includes the pisiform, hamate, capitate, trapezoid, and
trapezium. The pisiform does not articulate as part of the distal row proper but acts as a
sesamoid embedded within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon (Figure 1).
The distal radius articulates with the scaphoid and lunate, with two distinct fossae
separated by the interfacet prominence. The distal radius has a mean volar tilt of 10°,
with a mean ulnar inclination of the radial styloid of 24°.1 The distal ulna articulates with
the triquetrum via the triangular fibrocartilage complex.

The carpus is divided into proximal and distal rows. The midcarpal joint is the
articulation between the proximal and distal rows of the carpus. The proximal row is
described as an intercalated segment. Although no tendinous insertions on this row are
present, substantial motion exists within the row because of forces from neighboring
articulations. Conversely, the distal row has relatively strong interconnections via
intercarpal ligaments, with less motion within the row itself. Flexion-extension
movements of the wrist primarily occur at the articulation between the radius and the
proximal row.2 Radioulnar deviation of the wrist primarily occurs at the midcarpal joint.3
The midcarpal joint is described as containing three distinct zones. The most radial zone
involves the articulation between the distal pole of the scaphoid with the trapezoid and
trapezium (scaphotrapeziotrapezoid [STT] joint). The scaphoid also articulates with the
radial aspect of the capitate (scaphocapitate joint). The middle zone of the midcarpal
joint consists of the articulation between the lunate proximally and the capitate distally
(lunocapitate joint). Some variation exists with regard to the lunate articulation. In some
individuals, the lunate articulates with the capitate alone, described as a type I lunate by
Viegas et al.4 In other individuals, in addition to the capitate articulation, the lunate has a
medial articulation with the hamate, described as a type II lunate.4 Finally, the most
ulnar zone includes the articulation between the hamate and triquetrum (triquetral-
hamate joint).
Figure 1 Photographs of a cadaver model show the osseous anatomy of the wrist. A, The
scaphoid (S) and lunate (L) are shown. B, Cross-section of the carpus shows the
trapezium (TM), trapezoid (TZ), scaphoid (S), capitate (C), lunate (L), hamate (H),

Ligamentous Anatomy
Intrinsic ligaments originate and insert within the carpus within the same row or between
proximal and distal rows.
Extrinsic ligaments of the wrist originate on the radius or ulna and insert on the carpus.

Ligamentous Anatomy
Ligamentous anatomy of the wrist is complex, with connections within the carpus and to
the adjacent bones of the forearm and hand. Taleisnik5 divided carpal ligaments into
intrinsic and extrinsic groups. Intrinsic ligaments originate and insert from within the
carpus, whereas extrinsic ligaments connect the carpus to the radius or ulna6 (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Images show the ligamentous anatomy of the wrist. A, Arthroscopic image of
the volar wrist ligaments shows the radioscaphocapitate (RSC) ligament and the long
radiolunate (LRL) ligament. B, Photograph of an anatomic cadaver model shows the

volar wrist ligaments. The black dot represents the space of Poirier. C, Drawing of the
volar ligaments shows the RCR ligament, LRL ligament, short radiolunate (SRL) ligament,
and ulnocarpal (UC) ligament. D, Photograph of a cadaver model shows dissection of the
dorsal ligaments. E, Drawing of the dorsal ligaments shows the dorsal intercarpal
ligament (DIC) and the triquetral ligament (TL). (Courtesy of Moneim Moheb, MD,
Albuquerque, NM.)

Extrinsic Carpal Ligaments
The extrinsic ligaments of the wrist are divided into three major groups: volar
radiocarpal, volar ulnocarpal, and dorsal radiocarpal.
The four volar radiocarpal ligaments include the radioscaphoid, radioscaphocapitate,
long radiolunate, and short radiolunate ligaments. The radioscaphoid ligament
originates on the volar radial margin of the distal radius and inserts on the scaphoid
tuberosity. The radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments originate in the
same location but insert on the volar capitate and the lunate, respectively. The short
radiolunate ligament originates from the volar ulnar margin of the distal radius and
inserts on the lunate. The space of Poirier is formed by the divergence between the
radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments.
The dorsal radiotriquetral ligament, also known as the dorsal radiocarpal ligament, is a
broad, fan-shaped ligament that arises from the dorsal edge of the distal radius,
inserting on the dorsum of the triquetrum, with some fibers continuing to insert on the
lunate (Video 1).

Intrinsic Carpal Ligaments

Intrinsic Carpal Ligaments
The scapholunate interosseous complex consists of three structures: dorsal and volar
scapholunate ligaments and a membranous fibrocartilaginous membrane. Controversy
exists with regard to the contributions of these components to wrist stability. The dorsal
scapholunate ligament is the strongest, followed by the volar portion; the weakest
component is the membranous component.7 The ultimate role these parts play in
conferring stability clinically remains a subject of ongoing discussion, particularly the role
they play in the broader setting of the other intrinsic and the extrinsic carpal ligaments.
The lunotriquetral interosseous ligament also has dorsal and volar components with a
fibrocartilaginous membrane in between. The volar lunotriquetral ligament is stronger
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004029
6/30

than the dorsal ligament.
The dorsal intercarpal ligament originates from the dorsal ridge of the triquetrum and
crosses the distal edge of the lunate, inserting on the dorsal rim of the scaphoid,
trapezoid, and trapezium.
Epidemiology
Primary Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
The incidence of osteoarthritis without identifiable cause (idiopathic) increases with age.
The incidence is similar in men and women until menopause, after which the incidence is
higher in women.
A genetic predisposition may exist.

Primary Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
Primary (idiopathic) osteoarthritis is more common in older populations. With increasing
age, an increased opportunity for onset of a given condition exists; however, increased
time and use also may contribute to the development of osteoarthritis. Although
incidence is similar in men and women before menopause, a higher incidence is
observed in postmenopausal women compared with age-matched males. Patterns of
genetic predisposition exist, and incidence varies among racial and ethnic groups.
Although humans desire to arbitrarily divide patients or conditions into normal or
disease state or narrow buckets that represent a given pathology, conditions exist along
a spectrum. Although surgeons may consider inflammatory arthritis versus
osteoarthritis versus posttraumatic arthritis, joint status exists as a continuum, with
blurring at the edges. An example of this may be inflammatory osteoarthritis or a patient
with well controlled rheumatoid arthritis in whom osteoarthritis occurs at the
trapeziometacarpal joint (Resource 1).

A review of 1,007 wrist radiographs obtained from patients seeking care from a specialist
identified osteoarthritis in 47 patients. One-half were not in the pattern of scapholunate
advanced collapse (SLAC) or scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC).8
Secondary Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
SLAC and SNAC
Scaphoid Lunate Advanced Collapse
Occurs with chronic dissociation of the scaphoid and lunate9 (Figure 3)
History of trauma may or may not be recalled.1
Male predominance
Patients typically younger
Manual laborers
Bilaterality may be observed in patients with gout, lupus, or other conditions that cause
attrition of the scapholunate ligament

Scaphoid Nonunion Advanced Collapse
SLAC and SNAC are among the most common patterns of wrist arthritis.11 They share
similar epidemiologic characteristics because they are primarily associated with trauma,
which is most common among younger males. SLAC may less commonly occur in
association with other conditions that cause secondary osteoarthritis of the wrist and
that have the various epidemiologic characteristics specific to the underlying condition.
Figure 4 AP radiograph of a wrist with scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse. Joint space
narrowing is observed between the distal pole of the scaphoid and the radial styloid and
between the distal pole of the scaphoid and the trapezium and trapezoid. Minimal joint

Etiology
Primary Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
Idiopathic12 (Resource 2)
Possible genetic predisposition
Uncommon
More common with increasing age
Secondary Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
Posttraumatic
Crystal deposition disease
Metabolic bone disease
Osteonecrosis
Anatomic predisposition or uncorrected deformity

Secondary Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
Acute and chronic injuries, including intra-articular fractures and destabilizing injuries to
the ligaments or the radial joint articulations of the proximal carpal row, such as
scaphoid nonunion, and scapholunate ligamentous injury leading to malalignment, are
common causes of secondary osteoarthritis of the wrist, leading to SLAC and SNAC
wrist.13 Trauma also may lead to radiocarpal arthritis, which is primarily the result of
distal radial fractures with malunion of the joint surface. Surgeons must recognize that
radiographic evidence of arthritis has limited correlation with symptoms. Crystal
deposition diseases, such as gout, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
(pseudogout), and hydroxyapatite deposition disease, and metabolic diseases, such as
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004029
10/30

articular chondrocalcinosis, osteomalacia, Paget disease, gout, osteoporosis, and
osteogenesis imperfecta, are other substantial causes of secondary osteoarthritis of the
wrist that do not fall within the classification of SLAC and SNAC.13-15
Less common causes include primary osteonecrosis (Kienböck disease and Preiser
disease), and anatomic predisposition or uncorrected deformity (ie, Madelung
deformity). STT joint arthritis can occur because of laxity at the carpus, such as in
patients with scapholunate pathology or as a developmental finding, particularly with
ligamentous laxity, often in women. The STT joint becomes arthritic and locks the carpus.
Usually STT arthritis is asymptomatic; however, it occasionally is associated with
irritation of the flexor carpi radialis or attritional rupture). Surgeons must recognize STT
joint arthritis in patients with ligamentous laxity; if the trapezium is excised, the carpus
can become unlocked, leading to carpal malalignment that may be symptomatic.13-16
Pathophysiology
SLAC arthritis may occur after scapholunate interosseous ligament injury. With loss of
secondary stabilizers, palmar flexion (dorsal intercalated segment instability [DISI]) and
rotation of the scaphoid may occur, leading to abnormal wrist kinematics and a typical pattern
of arthritis.
Scaphoid nonunion leads to malalignment of the carpus and arthritis of the distal pole of the
scaphoid and radial styloid that also occurs predictably (SNAC).

Pathophysiology
SLAC can develop over a variable duration and produces variable symptoms. Injury to
the scapholunate interosseous ligament leads to palmar flexion of the scaphoid and
extension of the lunate, also known as DISI. Abnormal radioscaphoid rotatory loads lead
to radial styloid degeneration, which progresses to the entire radioscaphoid joint.17 As
the scapholunate interval increases, the capitate migrates proximally, contributing to
abnormal capitolunate loading. Altered intercarpal contact forces subsequently lead to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004029
11/30

arthritis of the capitolunate joint. In advanced cases, the remainder of the carpus
becomes involved, usually sparing the radiolunate joint.
Disruption of the scapholunate interosseous ligament causes DISI deformity.
Theoretically, injury to the lunotriquetral ligament can cause the lunate and scaphoid to
flex while the triquetrum extends, resulting in a volar intercalated segment instability
deformity.13 The lunotriquetral ligament, dorsal radiotriquetral ligament, and volar
radiolunate ligament must be injured to produce the deformity; however, most volar
intercalated segment instability is not associated with ligament insufficiency.
Lunotriquetral ligament rupture is uncommon and of uncertain importance.
SNAC is a pattern of arthritis that occurs because of arthritis of the distal scaphoid and
the radial styloid in patients with a scaphoid nonunion.18 Degeneration occurs first at
the radial side of the scaphoid and the radial styloid, then to the scaphocapitate joint,
and last to the scaphotrapezium and scaphotrapezoid joints.
Classification
Watson classification of SLAC19 (Figure 5)
Stage I: localized arthritis of the radioscaphoid joint in the radial styloid
Stage II: extensive involvement of the radioscaphoid joint, including the scaphoid fossa and
the radial styloid
Stage III: stage II with involvement of the capitolunate articulation
Stage IV: not part of original Watson classification pancarpal wrist arthritis.
Classification of SNAC13
Stage I: radial styloid affected
Stage II: stage I with scaphocapitate articulation affected
Stage III: stage II with capitolunate articulation affected
Stage IV: pancarpal wrist arthritis

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patients often present with wrist pain, decreased range of motion, and dorsal wrist swelling.
Bilateral wrist radiographs should be obtained.
CT, MRI, and diagnostic wrist arthroscopy are not performed, except for rare occasions to help
determine treatment options.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Wrist pain is the predominant symptom of SLAC/SNAC wrist; however, not all patients
with radiographic findings have pain.11 Patients also may present with decreased wrist
range of motion and dorsoradial wrist swelling or bony prominences. They may have a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004029
13/30

history of pseudogout, rheumatoid arthritis, amyloidosis, neuropathic disorders, or
scaphoid fracture.20,21
Bilateral PA, oblique, and lateral wrist radiographs can be obtained. DISI deformities can
be observed. In scapholunate injuries, the scapholunate gap is abnormal if it is greater
than 2 to 3 mm on PA radiographs (Figure 6). Moneim tangential radiographs may afford
adequate visualization of the scapholunate interval22 (Figure 7). Scaphoid nonunion can
be evaluated via a navicular radiograph (Figure 8). Patterns of cartilage degeneration
also can be observed to distinguish between various stages of SLAC/SNAC and basal joint
arthritis to aid in treatment decision making (Figure 3).

demonstrates an approximately 8-mm scapholunate gap. (Courtesy of Deana Mercer,
MD, Albuquerque, NM.)

greater than 10°, a capitolunate angle greater than 30°, and a scapholunate angle

plain radiography, especially for moderate arthritic changes in SLAC and SNAC; however,
MRI can underestimate cartilage degeneration24 (Figure 10).

CT can be performed specifically to stage SLAC/SNAC and evaluate for adjacent joint
degeneration, especially in earlier stages. Scaphoid nonunions also can be more clearly
defined on CT scans compared with plain radiographs (Figure 11).
Figure 11 Coronal CT scans of a wrist obtained 1 year after fixation of a scaphoid
fracture show different sections a scaphoid nonunion. (Courtesy of Deana Mercer, MD,
Albuquerque, NM.)
Wrist arthroscopy may be helpful for diagnostic as well as therapeutic purposes.
Surgeons can directly evaluate chondral defects and the extent of arthrosis in specific
joints and identify the integrity of ligamentous injuries.13 Arthroscopy can be performed
to débride synovitis, loose bodies, and address some chondral pathology. Studies report
imperfect resolution of pain; however, in some series, patients noted symptom
improvement despite not managing the mechanical problem in the wrist.25,26 The role of
surgical management intended to alleviate pain without addressing mechanical issues
(palliative surgery) is a subject of debate; currently, adequate research comparing this
intervention with placebo surgery is lacking.

Management
Nonsurgical management consists of acetaminophen, NSAIDs, splints, and corticosteroid
injection.
Surgical treatment options are considered if patients are unsatisfied with nonsurgical
treatment.
Salvage treatment options include the following:
Radial styloidectomy
Distal pole scaphoid excision
Limited wrist arthrodesis
Proximal row carpectomy
Total wrist arthrodesis
Treatment options open to debate
Anterior or posterior interosseous nerve neurectomy for palliative management
Wrist arthroplasty
Durability is limited in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and, therefore, is in question in
patients with posttraumatic arthritis.

Management
If patients are not satisfied with nonsurgical treatment options, surgical treatment may
be offered. Surgical treatment options vary based on the stage of arthritis and surgeon
and patient preferences.
One suggested approach is limited denervation, cutting the terminal branches of the
anterior and/or posterior interosseous nerves.27,28 This palliative surgical treatment
option has not been compared with placebo or simulated surgery and is a subject of
debate.
In patients with early (stage I) symptomatic SLAC/SNAC, radial styloidectomy is a salvage
(reconstructive) treatment option that may reduce pain. To maintain the
radioscaphocapitate ligament, styloidectomy should be limited to no more than 3 to 4
mm of the radial styloid via a short oblique osteotomy.29
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteoarthritis of the Wrist
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004029

In patients with early (stage I) SNAC, if the capitolunate joint and more than one-half of
the proximal pole of the scaphoid are preserved, distal pole scaphoid excision may be
considered.30
Partial arthrodesis of the lunate, capitate, hamate, and triquetrum with scaphoid
excision is a treatment option for the management of stage II and stage III SLAC/SNAC.
Headless compression screws, Kirschner wires, and circular plates have been used.31-33
Bone graft, often from the distal radius or the excised scaphoid, can be used to increase
the rate of union. Open and arthroscopic techniques have been described (Videos 2 and
3; Resource 3; Figure 12).

Proximal row carpectomy can be performed in patients with stage II disease if the
capitate and lunate facet are preserved. Benefits include no implants and no delay in
return to activity for bone healing. The entire proximal row of carpal bones in the wrist is
removed. This includes the removal of the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum, with
preservation of the radioscaphocapitate ligament, and the capitate articulates with the
lunate facet. Some surgeons express concern for progression of arthritis involving
capitate-radius articulation over a patient’s lifetime. Other surgeon feel such
considerations are relatively unimportant if patients are electing to undergo surgical
treatment for various levels and duration of pain relief and maintenance of wrist motion.
Patients may reconsider their treatment options over time as the pathology evolves, and
a definitive solution at a single point in time may not be the best manner in which to
conceptualize this process34 (Videos 4, 5 and 6; Figure 13).

multiple prior failed treatment attempts. Preoperative PA (A), oblique (B), and lateral (C)
radiographs. PA (D), oblique (E), and lateral (F) radiographs obtained after proximal row
carpectomy for pain. (Courtesy of Deana Mercer, MD, Albuquerque, NM.)
Partial arthrodesis and proximal row carpectomy decrease wrist motion and leave
abnormal articulations that may be a source of pain (Resource 4).
In patients with stage III or stage IV SLAC/SNAC, and in patients with earlier stages who
have limited wrist motion, total wrist arthrodesis affords reliable and durable pain
relief35 (Figure 14). Some surgeons plan arthrodesis of the third carpometacarpal joint
unless the plate will be removed after union is achieved for theoretic concern that
motion at this unfused joint may lead to pain or hardware failure; however, published
data support the practice of no attempted fusion of the third carpometacarpal joint and
hardware retention.36

The role of total wrist arthroplasty for posttraumatic osteoarthritis is a subject of
debate.37 Concerns regarding the longevity of the implant make this an attractive
treatment option only in low-demand or older patients who do not rely on assistive
devices for weight bearing. Total wrist arthroplasty for the management of
posttraumatic conditions should be considered experimental.
